headline: Tekubi is 手 (te, “hand”) plus 首 (kubi, “neck”).
Nakanaori is 仲 (naka, “relationship”) plus 直り (naori, “improving, being repaired”).
Nuu went from nupu to nuɸu to nuː, from Old Japanese.
Tansui is 淡 (“tasteless”) plus 水 (“water”).
Hieru is from the classical verb 冷ゆ (hiyu).
Hidoi is derived from 非道 (hidō, “evil, inhuman”) plus -i.
Tate is the nominalized form of the verb 立てる (tateru, “stand”).
Monooto is 物 (mono, “thing”) plus 音 (oto, “sound”).
Ōjiru shifted from the verb 応ずる (ōzuru).
Mōfu is probably an orthographic borrowing from Chinese 毛布 (máobù, literally “hair + cloth”), first cited in 1867 for wool fabric.
Nan, “difficulty”, is from Middle Chinese 難 (MC nan).
Binzume is 瓶 (bin, “bottle”) plus 詰め (tsume), the stem of 詰める (tsumeru, “to stuff”), with tsume voiced to zume.
Michiru is from Old Japanese 満つ (mitu), from Proto-Japonic *mit-.
In katana, 刀 first appears in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE, but the katana furigana appears only centuries later.
Kōyō began as kou jepu: Middle Chinese 紅葉, literally “crimson, red + leaf”.
Tenugui is 手 (te, “hand”) plus 拭い (nugui, “wiping; wiper”).
Meiwaku is from Middle Chinese 迷惑 (MC mej hwok).
Chikasui is 地下 (chika, “underground”) plus 水 (-sui, “water”).
Kotori is 小 (ko-, “little”) plus 鳥 (tori, “bird”), first attested in the late 900s in the Utsubo Monogatari.
Son, “loss”, is from Middle Chinese 損 (MC swonX).
Setomono is literally “Seto ware”: Seto City has long been famous for its earthenware.
Mafurā is borrowed from English muffler.
Teido is Middle Chinese 程度.
Ichiba is 市 (ichi, “market”) plus 場 (ba, “place”); compare English marketplace.
Kaeru, “to substitute”, is from Old Japanese かふ (kapu).
Chihō is from Middle Chinese 地方 (MC dijH pjang).
Deiriguchi is an abbreviated form of 出入り口.
Shōgai, “one's lifetime”, began as syaugai.
Yon is a shift from yo, influenced by analogy with the final sound of the preceding number 三 (san, “three”).
Kyanpu is English camp, a doublet of キャンパス (kyanpasu, “campus”).
Narubeku is なる (naru, “to become”) plus べく (beku, adverbial form of べし), first cited to the 1890s.
